### D.3 Adapting Baselines to the Budgeted Setting

WinMax (Kirchenbauer et al., 2024), WaterSeeker (Pan et al., 2025), and AOL (Zhao et al., 2025) were designed for the full-scan setting. They compute the watermark score of every token and localize watermarked segments from this dense score sequence. In our setting, the detector can be evaluated at no more than $B$ token positions. We therefore keep the localization rule of each method and change only how token scores are obtained. Each baseline evaluates the detector on a sparse subset of $B$ positions instead of all $N$ . It computes its statistics from the scores of the queried tokens only, and unqueried tokens are ignored rather than imputed. The budget fraction $B/N$ thus determines how densely each baseline scans the document, and $B=N$ recovers the original full-scan method. We refer to the adapted methods as B-WinMax, B-WaterSeeker, and B-AOL.

The three adaptations share a coarse-to-fine pattern. Part of the budget is spent on sparse probes spread evenly over the document. The rest is spent on positions that the method itself identifies as promising from these probes. The methods differ in how they identify those positions.

B-WinMax. WinMax scans windows of varying lengths and returns the window with the largest z-score. B-WinMax first probes the document at evenly spaced positions and computes each window’s z-score from the probed tokens inside it. It then spends the remaining budget on unqueried tokens in and around the highest-scoring windows, and recomputes the window scores as new tokens are queried. When the budget is exhausted, it reports the windows selected by the WinMax criterion from the sparse scores.

B-WaterSeeker. WaterSeeker first smooths the token scores to detect suspicious regions, and then traverses each region locally to determine its boundaries. B-WaterSeeker runs the first stage on sparse probes spread over the document. It spends the remaining budget on unqueried tokens within and around the suspicious regions. The local traversal is then carried out on the queried tokens, and the resulting segments are reported.

B-AOL. AOL treats the token scores as a noisy sequence and estimates its local mean with an adaptive online estimator. It reports the positions whose estimate exceeds a threshold. B-AOL applies the same estimator to the queried tokens in document order. It places subsequent queries in regions whose current estimate is high or close to the threshold, which refines the estimated segment boundaries. When the budget is exhausted, it reports the segments given by the final estimate.

In all three cases, the watermark detector and the cost of a query are the same as for BELL. Every method therefore evaluates the detector the same number of times at a given $B/N$ . The methods differ only in where they place their queries and in how they turn the queried scores into localized segments.

### D.4 Adapter Construction

We now discuss how watermark-specific detector outputs can be converted into e-evidence that is compatible with the statistical layer of BELL. A useful distinction is between the pure-null case $\theta_{0}=0$ and the general composite-null case $\theta_{0}>0$ .

When $\theta_{0}=0$ , every token in a null block is unwatermarked. In this case, standard likelihood-ratio or exponential-moment constructions can be applied directly at the token level. When $\theta_{0}>0$ , however, the block-level null hypothesis itself permits a nonzero fraction of watermarked tokens. Consequently, a token queried from a null block need not be an unwatermarked token, and a token-level e-value calibrated only under $z_{i}=0$ is no longer sufficient. In this regime, the adapter should be calibrated to the block-level composite null and may naturally depend on $\theta_{0}$ .

We first describe the standard adapters for $\theta_{0}=0$ , and then discuss several general strategies for constructing $\theta_{0}$ -dependent adapters.

Standard token-level adapters when $\theta_{0}=0$ . Let $\mathcal{G}_{t}$ denote all information available before the detector score of the current queried position is revealed, including all previously observed detector outputs and any round- $t$ tuning parameters. For watermark family $W$ , let $s_{i}^{W}$ denote the scheme-specific identifier determining the keyed randomization used to score position $i$ . This identifier may correspond, for example, to a context-dependent seed, a context code, or a key-coordinate index.

To avoid treating repeated keyed randomness as fresh statistical evidence, we associate each position with an eligibility indicator $\chi_{i}^{W}\in\{0,1\}$ . The eligibility indicator is determined before the corresponding keyed detector score is inspected. Positions for which the required adapter inputs are unavailable, or for which the same keyed randomization has already been used under the scoring rule, are assigned the neutral factor

$$ e_{i,t}^{W}=1. $$

For eligible positions, the constructions below satisfy

$$ \mathbb{E}[e_{i,t}^{W}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{W}=1]\leq 1. $$

All tuning parameters appearing below are either fixed before testing or are $\mathcal{G}_{t}$ -measurable, i.e., they are chosen before observing the current detector score.

Under $\theta_{0}=0$ , a null block contains only positions with $z_{i}=0$ . Therefore, the conditional validity in Eq. (10) is sufficient for multiplicative evidence accumulation.

KGW-style watermarking. Let

$$ Z_{i}^{\mathrm{KGW}}:=\mathbf{1}\{x_{i}\in G_{i}\}, $$

where $G_{i}$ is the keyed green list associated with position $i$ . For an eligible unwatermarked position, the null randomization satisfies

$$ Z_{i}^{\mathrm{KGW}}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{\mathrm{KGW}}=1\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\gamma), $$

where $\gamma\in(0,1)$ is the green-list inclusion probability.

For any predictable reference parameter $p_{t}^{\star}\in(\gamma,1)$ , define

$$ e_{i,t}^{\mathrm{KGW}}:=\left(\frac{p_{t}^{\star}}{\gamma}\right)^{Z_{i}^{\mathrm{KGW}}}\left(\frac{1-p_{t}^{\star}}{1-\gamma}\right)^{1-Z_{i}^{\mathrm{KGW}}}. $$

This is a likelihood-ratio e-value, and

$$ \mathbb{E}[e_{i,t}^{\mathrm{KGW}}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{\mathrm{KGW}}=1]=1. $$

The reference parameter $p_{t}^{\star}$ need not equal the true watermarked green-token probability; misspecification affects power but not null validity.

Hu-style unbiased reweighting. Let $P_{i}$ denote the reference next-token distribution and $Q_{i}$ the corresponding keyed reweighted distribution. For an eligible position, the unbiased-reweighting property gives

$$ \mathbb{E}[Q_{i}(x)\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,x_{i},P_{i},z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{\mathrm{Hu}}=1]=P_{i}(x) $$

for every token $x$ . We therefore define

$$ e_{i,t}^{\mathrm{Hu}}:=\frac{Q_{i}(x_{i})}{P_{i}(x_{i})},\qquad P_{i}(x_{i})>0. $$

It follows immediately that

$$ \mathbb{E}[e_{i,t}^{\mathrm{Hu}}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,x_{i},P_{i},z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{\mathrm{Hu}}=1]=1. $$

Positions for which $P_{i}(x_{i})=0$ or the required adapter inputs are unavailable are assigned the neutral factor in Eq. (9).

SynthID-style watermarking. Consider an eligible position with $K_{\mathrm{syn}}$ binary keyed layers

$$ g_{i,1},\ldots,g_{i,K_{\mathrm{syn}}}. $$

Under the null randomization,

$$ (g_{i,1},\ldots,g_{i,K_{\mathrm{syn}}})\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{\mathrm{Syn}}=1\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)^{\otimes K_{\mathrm{syn}}}. $$

For any predictable $\lambda_{t}\geq 0$ , define

$$ e_{i,t}^{\mathrm{Syn}}:=\exp\left\{\lambda_{t}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{syn}}}g_{i,k}-K_{\mathrm{syn}}\log\left(\frac{1+\exp(\lambda_{t})}{2}\right)\right\}. $$

The null moment-generating function gives

$$ \mathbb{E}[e_{i,t}^{\mathrm{Syn}}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{\mathrm{Syn}}=1]=1. $$

The $K_{\mathrm{syn}}$ keyed layers are treated jointly as one token-level observation.

Gumbel/exponential watermarking. Let $U_{i,x_{i}}$ denote the keyed uniform coordinate used by the local exponential-minimum detector, and define

$$ Z_{i}^{\mathrm{Exp}}:=-\log U_{i,x_{i}}. $$

For an eligible unwatermarked position,

$$ U_{i,x_{i}}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{\mathrm{Gum}}=1\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1), $$

and hence

$$ Z_{i}^{\mathrm{Exp}}\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1). $$

For any predictable $\lambda_{t}\geq 0$ , define

$$ e_{i,t}^{\mathrm{Gum}}:=(1+\lambda_{t})\exp\{-\lambda_{t}Z_{i}^{\mathrm{Exp}}\}. $$

Since

$$ \mathbb{E}[\exp\{-\lambda_{t}Z_{i}^{\mathrm{Exp}}\}]=\frac{1}{1+\lambda_{t}}, $$

we obtain

$$ \mathbb{E}[e_{i,t}^{\mathrm{Gum}}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t},a_{t}=i,z_{i}=0,\chi_{i}^{\mathrm{Gum}}=1]=1. $$

Accumulation under the pure null. For $\theta_{0}=0$ , every position in a null block satisfies $z_{i}=0$ . Therefore, if block $j$ is queried at rounds

$$ \mathcal{T}_{j}(t):=\{s\leq t:j_{s}=j\}, $$

the product

$$ E_{j}(t):=\prod_{s\in\mathcal{T}_{j}(t)}e_{s} $$

is a nonnegative e-process under $H_{j,0}$ , provided the local conditional-validity condition is maintained at every query. Consequently,

$$ \mathbb{E}[E_{j}(\tau)\mid H_{j,0}]\leq 1 $$

for any bounded stopping time $\tau$ generated by the adaptive query history.

Why $\theta_{0}>0$ is different. The situation changes fundamentally when the block-level null is

$$ H_{j,0}:\theta_{j}\leq\theta_{0},\qquad\theta_{0}>0. $$

Writing

$$ K_{j}:=\lfloor\theta_{0}L_{j}\rfloor, $$

the null now permits as many as $K_{j}$ genuinely watermarked positions inside block $j$ . Thus, even when $H_{j,0}$ is true, a queried position may satisfy $z_{i}=1$ .

This observation is important because the standard adapters in Eqs. (13)–(23) are calibrated under $z_{i}=0$ . In general,

$$ \mathbb{E}[e_{i,t}^{W}\mid z_{i}=1] $$

may be substantially larger than one. Therefore, simply multiplying the $\theta_{0}=0$ token-level e-values does not in general yield a valid e-value for the composite null in Eq. (27).

More generally, there is no reason to require that every individual query be an e-value for the entire block-level composite null. For $\theta_{0}>0$ , it is often more natural to construct a $\theta_{0}$ -dependent block-level e-process

$$ E_{j,t}^{(\theta_{0})}=\mathcal{A}_{W}^{(\theta_{0})}(Z_{j,1:t};L_{j},K_{j}), $$

whose validity requirement is directly

$$ \sup_{\theta_{j}\leq\theta_{0}}\mathbb{E}[E_{j,\tau}^{(\theta_{0})}]\leq 1. $$

Here $\tau$ may be the adaptively determined number of queries allocated to block $j$ . The allocation layer of BELL can still use local detector scores or predictable evidence surrogates to decide where to query; only the terminal block-level quantity used by e-BH needs to satisfy Eq. (30).

Different choices of $\theta_{0}$ therefore naturally induce different adapters. Below we outline several useful constructions.

Insight 1: finite-population likelihood adapters. Suppose that a watermark-specific score $Y$ admits a conditional model

$$ Y\mid z=0\sim P_{0},\qquad Y\mid z=1\sim P_{1}, $$

or, more generally, $P_{1}$ belongs to a specified family $\mathcal{P}_{1}$ .

Assume queried locations within a selected block are sampled uniformly without replacement. Conditional on a block containing exactly $k$ watermarked positions, the latent provenance sequence of the queried tokens then follows a finite-population sampling law. Let

$$ p_{j,t}^{(k,\eta)}(Y_{1:t}) $$

denote the likelihood of the first $t$ queried scores when block $j$ contains exactly $k$ watermarked positions and $\eta$ denotes any nuisance parameter governing the watermarked-score distribution.

A reference alternative can be formed by mixing over $k>K_{j}$ :

$$ Q_{j,t}:=\sum_{\ell=K_{j}+1}^{L_{j}}\pi_{\ell}p_{j,t}^{(\ell,\eta_{\ell})},\qquad\sum_{\ell=K_{j}+1}^{L_{j}}\pi_{\ell}=1. $$

A composite-null e-value is then obtained by

$$ E_{j,t}^{\mathrm{LR}}:=\frac{Q_{j,t}}{\displaystyle\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq k\leq K_{j}\\
\eta\in\mathcal{H}_{0}\end{subarray}}p_{j,t}^{(k,\eta)}}. $$

For every null model $(k_{0},\eta_{0})$ ,

$$ E_{j,t}^{\mathrm{LR}}\leq\frac{Q_{j,t}}{p_{j,t}^{(k_{0},\eta_{0})}}. $$

The quantity on the right is a likelihood-ratio process under the corresponding simple null. Hence Eq. (34) is valid uniformly over the composite null, provided the null family contains the true score law.

This construction is attractive because it treats $\theta_{j}\leq\theta_{0}$ directly as a finite-population hypothesis rather than repeatedly protecting each individual query against the worst possible provenance assignment. The likelihood $p_{j,t}^{(k,\eta)}$ can be evaluated by a simple dynamic program over the latent number of queried watermarked positions.

Insight 2: finite-population MGF and bounded-score adapters. Exact likelihood models for watermarked positions may not always be available. A weaker alternative is to characterize the moment-generating behavior of a score statistic $T$ .

Suppose that, for a fixed $\lambda$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\log\mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda T)\mid z=0] \displaystyle\leq\psi_{0}^{+}(\lambda), \displaystyle\log\mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda T)\mid z=1] \displaystyle\leq\psi_{1}^{+}(\lambda). $$

Consider a uniformly sampled batch of $h$ positions from a block of length $L_{j}$ . If the block contains exactly $k$ watermarked positions, the number $S$ of watermarked positions in the batch follows

$$ S\sim\operatorname{Hypergeom}(L_{j},k,h). $$

Hence a valid composite-null normalizer is

$$ \begin{split}M_{j,h}^{+}(\lambda):={}&\max_{0\leq k\leq K_{j}}\sum_{s}\frac{\binom{k}{s}\binom{L_{j}-k}{h-s}}{\binom{L_{j}}{h}}\\
&\quad\times\exp\{s\psi_{1}^{+}(\lambda)+(h-s)\psi_{0}^{+}(\lambda)\}.\end{split} $$

This yields the batch-level e-value

$$ E_{j,h}^{\mathrm{MGF}}:=\frac{\exp\{\lambda\sum_{r=1}^{h}T_{r}\}}{M_{j,h}^{+}(\lambda)}. $$

A particularly robust special case requires no explicit distributional model for watermarked positions. Suppose a nonnegative raw factor $R_{i}$ satisfies

$$ \mathbb{E}[R_{i}\mid z_{i}=0]\leq 1,\qquad 0\leq R_{i}\leq c $$

for some finite $c\geq 1$ . For a uniformly sampled batch of size $h$ , define

$$ C_{j,h}(c):=\sum_{s}\frac{\binom{K_{j}}{s}\binom{L_{j}-K_{j}}{h-s}}{\binom{L_{j}}{h}}c^{s}, $$

where the sum is over feasible $s$ . Then

$$ E_{j,h}^{\mathrm{cap}}:=\frac{\prod_{r=1}^{h}R_{r}}{C_{j,h}(c)} $$

is valid under any fixed provenance mask satisfying $\sum_{i\in I_{j}}z_{i}\leq K_{j}$ .

The finite-population normalization in Eq. (42) uses the fact that the null has a global budget of at most $K_{j}$ watermarked positions. This can be considerably less conservative than repeatedly treating every query as if the full contamination budget were still available. The batch size and any tuning parameters must be chosen before observing the scores in that batch.

Insight 3: mixtures can adapt to unknown watermark strength. The alternative watermark intensity is typically unknown. Even when $\theta_{0}$ is fixed, blocks under the alternative may have very different values of $\theta_{j}$ . An adapter therefore need not commit to a single alternative intensity or a single tuning parameter.

For example, the alternative likelihood in Eq. (33) may place mass on several candidate intensities,

$$ \pi_{\ell}\propto\pi(\ell/L_{j}),\qquad\ell>K_{j}, $$

so that the resulting e-value accumulates evidence across a range of possible watermark strengths.

Similarly, if $E_{j,t}(\lambda)$ is a valid e-value for every fixed $\lambda$ , then a fixed or predictable mixture

$$ E_{j,t}^{\mathrm{mix}}:=\int E_{j,t}(\lambda)\,d\Pi(\lambda) $$

remains valid. Such mixtures can reduce sensitivity to a single hand-tuned value of $p^{\star}$ or $\lambda$ while preserving the statistical guarantee.

More generally, the amount of structure imposed on the watermarked-position distribution determines a robustness–power tradeoff. A large null family $\mathcal{P}_{1}$ provides stronger robustness but typically yields more conservative evidence. A more informative family can substantially improve power, provided that the assumed family still contains the true score distribution.

Summary. The standard adapters in Eqs. (13)–(23) provide a simple and general interface when $\theta_{0}=0$ . For $\theta_{0}>0$ , however, the null hypothesis permits genuine watermarked tokens and therefore requires a $\theta_{0}$ -aware calibration.

The key point is that BELL does not fundamentally require every queried token to produce an individually valid e-value. What is required by the terminal multiple-testing layer is a valid block-level e-value,

$$ \sup_{\theta_{j}\leq\theta_{0}}\mathbb{E}[E_{j}(B)]\leq 1. $$

Finite-population likelihood ratios, MGF-based constructions, bounded score calibrations, and mixtures provide several principled ways to construct such adapters. The appropriate choice depends on how much is known about the detector-score distribution for the corresponding watermark family.

### E.4 Explainability Experiment

To further understand why BELL achieves higher query efficiency, we extend the explainability analysis in Figure 2 to the remaining model–dataset configurations. We consider two complementary metrics introduced in Section 5.3. The Target Query Ratio (TQR) measures the fraction of queries allocated to ground-truth watermarked regions, reflecting whether the query budget is concentrated on relevant blocks. Evidence Gain measures the average positive log-evidence obtained per query, characterizing how much useful watermark evidence is extracted from each detector evaluation. Higher values of these two metrics therefore indicate more targeted query allocation and more effective evidence acquisition, respectively.
